Compare the options
Compare without getting lost in the numbers.
Compare night and face photos in a test, not just the name of the feature. A large sensor gives AI a better starting point.
Compare tests of the same laptop, not just the badge. And always separate the processor from the graphics card.
Compare the RAM with the chip, the storage and the software. For an Android or iOS phone, memory behavior can differ despite similar figures.
Compare the capacity, the storage standard if stated, expandability and the real weight of your files. Don’t pay for a very high capacity without a matching use.
Compare the capacity, then endurance measurements obtained with known protocols. Identical mAh values don’t mean identical battery life.
Compare measured brightness, refresh range, adaptive behavior, HDR and, where available, calibration measurements. For outdoor use, real legibility matters more than the name of the technology alone.
Compare the standard when the difference between two models is significant. Never confuse UFS with capacity expressed in GB.
Compare the standard, the supported bands and the quality of the connection in your environment rather than the theoretical maximum value.
Compare the operating range, the maximum rate, the modes used in games and the automatic behavior, rather than the maximum value alone.
Compare the glass protection, parts availability, repair cost and your usage environment. A tougher material doesn’t remove the risk of breakage.
Compare real power, the standard, compatibility with your accessories and thermal behavior.
Compare the exact code and the manufacturer’s conditions. Don’t turn IP68 into permission to use the phone underwater without precautions.
Compare the stated weight and dimensions. A built-in cable is handy but also wears out. For earbuds or a watch, look for a low-power mode.
Compare equivalent focal lengths, sensor sizes, stabilization and quality at different zoom levels.
Compare the features actually supported by the phone and your accessories. The version number isn’t enough.
Compare supported formats, luminance and independent measurements rather than treating HDR as a simple yes/no flag.
Compare measurement methods, typical brightness and real outdoor legibility. The biggest claimed number isn’t necessarily the most comfortable in direct sunlight.
Compare measured charging times, the protocol used, the compatible charger and thermal limits, not just the maximum value printed on the box.
Compare aperture, sensor, stabilization and real examples together. A single f-number can’t predict night quality.
Compare which sensors actually benefit from OIS and look at night examples. The presence of the acronym doesn’t predict all video behavior.
Above all, compare compatibility with your payment, access or identification service.
